summary: This section explains who has the legal right to ask the Tribunal to close down a company. It sets out the rules for different people like the company itself, shareholders, and government officials to file a winding up petition. It also outlines specific conditions they must follow, such as giving notices or submitting required statements.
points: The company, any contributory, the Registrar, or an authorised person can present a petition to wind up a company.
A contributory can file a petition even if they hold fully paid-up shares or if the company has no assets left.
The Registrar needs previous permission from the Central Government before filing a petition.
A company must include a statement of affairs when it presents a winding up petition.
A copy of the petition must be filed with the Registrar, who will submit views to the Tribunal.
example: Meera Textiles Private Limited was facing heavy debts and could no longer continue its business operations. Rohan, a shareholder who held fully paid-up shares registered in his name for over six months, decided to take action. Even though the company had no assets left to distribute, Rohan had the legal right to present a petition to the Tribunal for winding up the company. Meanwhile, the company also prepared its petition along with a statement of affairs. A copy of this petition was duly filed with the Registrar so that the Registrar could submit official views to the Tribunal within the given time.

terms.meaning: A special judicial body that handles company law cases.
A person liable to contribute to the assets of a company in the event of its being wound up, which includes shareholders.
A government authority appointed to keep company records and handle administrative duties under the Act.

watch: People often confuse whether a shareholder with fully paid-up shares can file for winding up, but the law clearly allows it under specific conditions.
